name: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate
lead: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate (MAP) is a water-soluble derivative of vitamin C used as an ingredient in skincare products, where it is marketed as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid. It is described in the literature as a pro-drug of vitamin C, meaning it is meant to be converted to ascorbic acid after reaching the skin. [3]

Laboratory work has found that ascorbic acid and its derivatives are more stable as ascorbyl esters than as the free acid in solution and in topical formulations. [4] A cosmetic ingredient safety review covering ascorbic acid and several of its salts and phosphate esters, including MAP, was published in the International Journal of Toxicology in 2005. [6]

Evidence for MAP on appearance outcomes includes small clinical studies of skin hydration, solar lentigines (age spots) and melasma. A split-face study of a 3% MAP moisturizer reported a reduction in the area of hyperpigmented spots [15], and trials in melasma have tested 5% MAP alongside a chemical peel or pulsed light [14][16]. Broader reviews of topical vitamin C note that clinical studies on formulated products are limited and that stability and penetration are the main formulation challenges [5].

paras: MAP appears in serums, creams and masks marketed for brightening, antioxidant protection and anti-aging. Reviews of topical vitamin C describe antioxidant, photoprotective, collagen-related and pigment-reducing effects for the vitamin as a class, though these reviews note that clinical data on formulated topical products are limited. [5]

For appearance, MAP is used mainly in leave-on serums, gels and moisturizers aimed at dull tone, dark spots and post-acne or sun-related marks. The chain people describe is: a stable vitamin C derivative is applied daily, is converted to ascorbic acid in skin, interferes with melanin formation and supports antioxidant defence, and over weeks the complexion looks more even and brighter [5][18]. A 2026 systematic review of vitamin C derivatives in dermatology states that ascorbic acid remains the most clinically validated form and discusses derivatives, including MAP, within that wider picture [17].

Vitamin C is described in reviews as reducing melanin formation, which is the basis for its use against hyperpigmentation [5]. A laboratory study reported that vitamin C and its derivatives acidify the interior of melanocytes, a mechanism linked to reduced melanin production and antioxidant effects [18].

Clinical studies have paired MAP cream with a trichloroacetic acid peel [14] and with fluorescent pulsed light [16]. Delivery research has also examined lasers, microdermabrasion and microneedles as ways to increase MAP penetration into skin [3][10].

L-ascorbic acid is unstable in solution, which motivated the development of derivatives. A 1997 analytical study found that ascorbyl palmitate and MAP were more stable than ascorbic acid in standard solutions and topical formulations. [4]

Percutaneous absorption research on pig skin examined ascorbic acid and its derivatives to define formulation features that deliver vitamin C into skin. [2] An in vitro study found that lasers and microdermabrasion increased skin permeation of vitamin C and also examined MAP delivery. [3] A 2019 study reported that hyaluronic acid microneedles were fabricated to enhance MAP delivery into skin. [10]

A Cosmetic Ingredient Review-style safety assessment of ascorbic acid, its calcium, magnesium and sodium salts, and magnesium and sodium ascorbyl phosphate, as used in cosmetics, was published in 2005. [6] Individual products carry their own label warnings, for example external use only and avoiding eye contact.
The pulsed-light melasma study reported the MAP combination as well tolerated [16]. MAP products are sold without prescription as cosmetics.

A study comparing ascorbic acid, MAP and ascorbyl tetra-isopalmitate applied to forearm skin for four weeks in volunteers reported that all formulations increased stratum corneum hydration; only the ascorbic acid product changed transepidermal water loss, and the MAP product changed a skin elasticity ratio. The authors concluded MAP improved hydration while derivatives did not match ascorbic acid on water loss. In laboratory antioxidant tests in the same study, ascorbic acid was strongest in the water-based system [7].

In a split-face study of 120 Japanese women aged 25 to 60 with solar lentigines, a moisturizer containing 3% MAP was applied to one side of the face and vehicle to the other for six months, with imaging at 1, 3 and 6 months and again six months after stopping. The authors reported a significant reduction in the total area of hyperpigmented spots while normal skin colour was maintained [15].

A randomized trial in Peshawar of 148 patients with epidermal melasma (74 per group, Fitzpatrick skin types III to V) compared a weekly 20% trichloroacetic acid peel with the peel plus 5% MAP cream daily for six weeks, after two weeks of tretinoin priming and with sunscreen. A significant MASI reduction was seen in 81.1% of the combination group versus 66.2% with the peel alone (p=0.040) [14].

An open study in Asian patients with refractory melasma combined 5% MAP for 12 weeks with three fluorescent pulsed light sessions. Among the 65 who completed it, mean MASI fell from 14.80 to 4.53 at week 12 and was 6.35 at week 24; the authors reported the combination was well tolerated and that maintenance treatment would be needed for persistent improvement [16].

A 2022 study formulated MAP in ethosomal and niosomal gels and compared them split-face in melasma patients using an Antera 3D camera. The ethosomal gel showed a statistically significant melanin decrease after one month and the niosomal gel after six months [13].
Registered clinical trials listing MAP also include dental gel studies for periodontitis and peri-implantitis [11][12].

card.summary: A stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative in brightening serums; common in products, thin on direct human trials.
card.note: Human data specific to MAP are sparse; most vitamin C evidence concerns L-ascorbic acid.

quick.overview:
Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a vitamin C derivative used in cosmetic serums and creams. It is promoted as being more stable than pure ascorbic acid.

Published evidence for its appearance effects is limited; one small study reported improved skin hydration, and reviews say clinical data on topical vitamin C are limited overall.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a pro-drug that is converted to ascorbic acid in skin. Laboratory studies show it is more stable than ascorbic acid in formulations, while penetration into skin is the main challenge discussed in the literature.
quick.risks: A cosmetic safety assessment covering MAP was published in 2005. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold without prescription; product labels advise external use and avoiding the eyes.
